title: How generative AI works — a useful mental model
body_md:
## A useful model: plausible output is not evidence

A generative model learns patterns from examples and uses a prompt to produce new text, sound, images or video. A language model predicts successive pieces of text; image and audio systems use different methods to synthesize media. You need not know their internals to handle a suspicious request. The important separation is **appearance versus authority**: a convincing sentence or familiar face says little about who controls the account, call or payment instruction.

A fraudster can combine public details with generated wording or media. The detail may be accurate and the request fraudulent. Conversely, an honest person may use an AI writing tool, translation, a noisy connection or a video filter. Do not classify people from grammar, accent, fingers or lip movement. Those cues can prompt a closer look, but they cannot authenticate a person. There is no stable minimum audio clip length that guarantees either a successful or impossible voice clone; quality depends on the tool and recording.

**Work backward from the action.** Identify what the message asks you to change: send money, reveal a code, change bank details, open a link, keep a secret. Then ask what independent route would confirm that action. Open a contact or app you already know, not a callback link or number supplied by the request. If the request concerns company funds, follow the documented approval route even when the person appears on video. A compromised real account can send a fraudulent request too.

This model has limits. Verification can fail if you choose a number from the suspicious message, an attacker controls multiple channels, or the real person is unreachable. In that case pause the irreversible action and use another trusted contact or your organisation's escalation procedure. Verification is a decision process, not a verdict on whether a file was generated.

### A one-minute routine

Name the requested action; stop before money or credentials move; leave the incoming channel; confirm through an independently found route; document the outcome if work policy requires it. The routine works for an ordinary impersonator as well as AI-assisted fraud.

widget_config.goal: Separate convincing AI-generated appearance from verified authority before acting on a request.
widget_config.today_action: Write down one trusted callback route for a person or team whose urgent request you might receive.
widget_config.scope: General educational guidance for personal and workplace requests, checked 20 October 2026; specific approval and emergency procedures vary.

sources.title: FTC: Scammers Use Fake Emergencies To Steal Your Money
sources.scope: US consumer advice, September 2023; voice cloning, urgency, independent callback and another relative. The US reporting route is jurisdiction-specific.

sources.title: FBI IC3: Business Email Compromise
sources.scope: US guidance for transfer and account-change requests; secondary-channel verification and urgent bank contact after a suspected transfer. Organisational and national procedures vary.

sources.title: NIST: 2024 GenAI text-to-text pilot
sources.scope: Published June 2025; benchmark on generated and human summaries, with detector performance varying by systems. It does not validate a detector for an individual message.

blocks.title: A perfect voice asks for a transfer
blocks.situation: A synthetic call sounds like the treasurer and asks you to send a supplier payment to a new account while the office is closed.
blocks.analysis: Voice resemblance and knowledge of the supplier can come from public or stolen material. The account change is the decision point. Hold it and call the treasurer or supplier on a number already on file, then use the normal approval path.

blocks.title: A translated, awkward message is real
blocks.situation: Synthetic example: A colleague uses translation software to report a delayed shipment. The phrasing is oddly formal, but the message only asks you to read a ticket already present in your work system.
blocks.analysis: Awkward wording does not make the message fraudulent. Open the work system independently and inspect the existing ticket; do not accuse the colleague or use an AI-text score as identity proof.

blocks.title: The convincing video request
blocks.setup: Synthetic scenario: a project manager appears on a video call about a rush vendor payment. The same request arrived in chat. Each decision is a separate snapshot; actions in one do not carry into the next. No real accounts or payments are involved.

steps.prompt: The face and voice match. What do you evaluate first?

choices.text: The requested change to payment details
choices.consequence: You identify the irreversible step before trusting the presentation.
choices.explanation: The risk lies in approving a new destination for funds; the media only delivers the request.

choices.text: Whether the video has a lip-sync error
choices.consequence: No artifact appears, so the transfer pressure remains.
choices.explanation: Clean video does not prove who controls the meeting.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: the manager posts a callback number in chat. Which route do you use?

choices.text: Use the manager number in the existing staff directory
choices.explanation: An independently stored contact is a separate check; the pasted number is part of the request.

choices.text: Use the new number; it is faster
choices.consequence: The same actor can answer and repeat the story.
choices.explanation: A second medium is not independent when its address comes from the first.

steps.prompt: Separate snapshot: you call the manager using the existing staff directory, but nobody answers. The deadline for the new-account payment is near. What now?

choices.text: Pause payment and escalate through the usual approver
choices.consequence: The payment waits while an authorised person checks it.
choices.explanation: An unanswered callback is not approval; established controls still apply.

choices.text: Approve because the video looked normal
choices.consequence: The unverified new account receives the funds in this simulation.
choices.explanation: Appearance cannot replace approval. Retry the decision using the existing route.

blocks.debrief: The key was the payment change. A model might be involved, but you do not need to prove that to protect the transaction. Retry any decision to see how the result changes.

questions.prompt: A real account sends a strange request for a new beneficiary. What matters?

choices.text: Verify the account change through the established process
choices.explanation: A real account can be compromised; the high-risk action still needs independent approval.

choices.text: Trust it because the account is genuine
choices.explanation: Account ownership at one moment does not prove the current message is authorised.

questions.prompt: An odd accent appears on a call without a money request. What does it prove?

choices.explanation: Connection quality, translation and individual variation can all affect sound.
Accent alone is not a reliable deepfake test.

questions.prompt: The caller gives you a second phone number to verify them. Is that independent?

choices.text: No; find a number already stored independently
choices.explanation: The attacker can control both the call and the newly supplied number.

choices.text: Yes; two phone numbers always establish identity
choices.explanation: Different numbers are not independent if both came from the same request.
